etymology: Clipped from professional, in sporting use since the nineteenth century (a "pro" as opposed to an amateur). Gaming culture of the 2000s–2020s made "pro" the highest praise for skill — esports professionals, "pro players," and the meme "pro gamer move" for a clever (often sneaky) trick. For Gen Alpha, "pro" is simply the opposite of "noob": "He’s a pro at Fortnite," "I’m pro at this," and "pro" as an adjective for anything done skillfully.
biblical_def: In Gen Alpha talk a pro is someone very good at something — especially a game. Calling yourself "pro" is a boast; calling a friend "pro" is a compliment. The Christian observation: skill is a gift of God, and Scripture praises it. The Psalmist says to "play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psa 33:3), and Bezaleel’s craftsmanship came from the Spirit of God. Work done with excellence honors the Lord: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23); "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). So it is good to want to be a pro. But Scripture also keeps a child humble about his skill: "For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" (1Co 4:7), and a man should not "think of himself more highly than he ought to think" (Rom 12:3). And it asks what we are getting good at. A child who is a pro at Fortnite and a beginner at kindness has practiced in the wrong order. A father can tell a five-year-old: "God made you able to get really good at things — that’s a gift from Him! Let’s get to be pros at loving people and helping, too." The best pro is the one who says thank you to the Giver.
webster_summary: Clip of professional (19th-c. sport; gaming 2000s-) — Gen Alpha’s word for skill, a gift Scripture praises when it is done heartily unto the Lord and held humbly as received.
webster_full: PRO, n. / a. (clip of professional; gaming usage 2000s–present; Gen Alpha) A highly skilled player; skillful. "She’s pro at Minecraft."
Pro gamer move — meme phrase for a clever or sneaky trick.
Opposite: noob, bot, default.
Decode for parents: a harmless compliment, sometimes a boast.
Webster 1828, the root — PROFESSIONAL, a. Pertaining to a profession or to a calling; as professional studies, pursuits, duties, engagements; professional character or skill.
scriptures: Psa 33:3
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
Rom 12:3

For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, according as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith.
corruption_summary: "Pro" praises real skill, which is God’s gift; it turns sour only as a boast, or when a child is a pro at the trivial and a beginner at the weighty.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in a word that praises excellence. The temptation is pride: the pro who looks down on the noob, the boast that forgets the gift. A secondary danger is disordered practice — the hours that make a child a pro at a game while the skills of home, school, and church go untended.

Praise excellence and ask what it serves. Teach the child to do everything heartily as to the Lord, to thank God for the ability, and to help the beginner. A pro who teaches a noob is living Romans 12.
roots_summary: Latin professio (public declaration) → English professional → sporting clip pro (19th c.) → gaming praise word (2000s–2020s).
usage: "Dad, you’re actually kind of pro at this."
Play skilfully — be a pro unto the Lord (Psa 33:3; Col 3:23).
What hast thou that thou didst not receive? Even your pro skills (1Co 4:7).

etymology: From hack, to chop. In 1950s–60s MIT student slang a hack was a clever trick and a hacker an ingenious programmer; by the 1980s the press used the word for criminals who break into computer systems. In Gen Alpha game usage a hacker is a cheater — someone using "hacks" (aimbots, wall-hacks, speed or fly exploits, modded clients) — and "HACKER!" is shouted at anyone who wins too well, cheater or not.
biblical_def: To a Gen Alpha child a hacker is a cheater in a game — someone using secret tricks to see through walls, aim automatically, or fly. Kids also yell "hacker!" at anyone who beats them, fair or not. The Christian observation: the word holds two sins, and Scripture names both. The first is cheating. "Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD; and a false balance is not good" (Pro 20:23). Paul uses an athlete’s rule: a man "is not crowned, except he strive lawfully" (2Ti 2:5). A game win stolen by hacks is no win at all, and a child who cheats in small things is practicing for large ones: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much" (Luk 16:10). The second sin is the false accusation. Calling someone a hacker because he beat you is bearing false witness: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour" (Exo 20:16). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Cheating is never okay, even in a game — God likes fair play. And we don’t say someone cheated just because they won. We say ‘good game.’" Teach both halves together: play fair, and accuse fairly.
webster_summary: From MIT’s clever programmer to the press’s computer criminal to Gen Alpha’s word for a game cheater — and the false cry of "hacker" at an honest winner; Scripture forbids both the false balance and the false witness.
webster_full: HACKER, n. (computing, 1960s; Gen Alpha game usage, 2010s–present) A cheater who uses exploits or cheat software in a game; loosely, any player suspected of cheating. "That guy’s a hacker — he’s flying."
Hacks — cheat tools: aimbot, wall-hack, speed hack, fly hack.
Older senses: an ingenious programmer (MIT, 1960s); a person who breaks into computer systems (1980s-).
Decode for parents: two lessons in one word — don’t cheat, and don’t falsely accuse.
Webster 1828, the root — HACK, v.t. To cut irregularly and into small pieces; to notch; to mangle by repeated strokes of a cutting instrument.
scriptures: Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD; and a false balance is not good.
And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
corruption_summary: Hacker names the cheater who strives unlawfully, and in a sore loser’s mouth it becomes a false witness; Scripture condemns the false balance and the false report alike.
corruption_paragraphs: Children cheat in games for the same reason adults cheat at taxes: the reward without the work, and the belief that no one is hurt. Every hack takes something from the other players, and every hack trains the conscience to ignore small injustice. Luke 16:10 is the law of character formation.

The accusation side is just as formative. A child who calls "hacker" whenever he loses is learning to explain away defeat by slandering the winner. Teach him to say "good game," to check before he accuses, and to strive lawfully even when it costs him the round.
roots_summary: Old English haccian (to chop) → hack (clever trick, MIT 1950s–60s) → hacker (programmer; then intruder, 1980s) → Gen Alpha game cheater.
roots_lines: 1950s–60s MIT slang: a hack, a clever trick; a hacker, an ingenious programmer
2000s–2020s gaming: hacks and hackers = cheats and cheaters
Gen Alpha: "HACKER!" at any suspiciously good player
usage: "He’s not hacking, bro, he’s just good."
He is not crowned, except he strive lawfully — no hacks (2Ti 2:5).
Thou shalt not bear false witness — don’t yell hacker at the winner (Exo 20:16).

etymology: A compound of try + hard, from the older insult "trying too hard." Gaming culture of the 2010s made tryhard the label for a player who takes a casual game too seriously — always using the strongest strategy, never playing for fun — and Gen Alpha uses it, along with sweat and sweaty, for anyone visibly giving full effort: at recess, in class, even at a board game. The word carries the youth-culture ideal that the coolest effort is invisible effort.
biblical_def: A tryhard is someone who tries too hard — in Gen Alpha usage, a player who is way too serious, or any kid who visibly cares a lot. "Stop being such a tryhard" means "relax, it’s just a game." Sometimes that rebuke is fair: winning at all costs, ruining the fun for everyone, is a kind of pride. Scripture warns against doing anything "through strife or vainglory" (Php 2:3). But the word often mocks something good: real effort. The Bible does not praise the cool shrug; it praises zeal. "Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord" (Rom 12:11). "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). And it saves its sharpest words for the lukewarm: "because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth" (Rev 3:16). A Christian child may be a "tryhard" in the best sense — at school, at practice, at prayer — without apology. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Trying hard is good — God loves it when we do our best! We just remember to be kind and have fun with our friends, too." He can teach the older child the difference: try hard to do well, never try hard to beat people down.
webster_summary: Gaming insult for one who plays too seriously (2010s) — sometimes a fair rebuke of vainglory, more often a sneer at zeal, which Scripture commands and the lukewarm lack.
webster_full: TRYHARD, n. / a. (gaming slang, 2010s–present; Gen Alpha) One who plays a casual game too seriously; one who visibly tries hard. "He’s tryharding in a pub match."
Synonyms: sweat, sweaty. Verb: to tryhard.
From the older phrase "trying too hard."
Decode for parents: listen for whether it rebukes a sore winner or mocks a hard worker.
Webster 1828, the root — TRY, v.i. To experience; to have knowledge by experience of.
scriptures: Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
corruption_summary: Tryhard rightly mocks the win-at-all-costs spirit, and wrongly mocks effort itself; the cool shrug it prizes is near to the lukewarmness Christ spues out.
corruption_paragraphs: Youth culture prizes effortless excellence and despises visible striving; tryhard is one of its enforcement words. Children learn to hide their effort, to pretend not to care, and to mock the classmate who raises his hand. That is a formation toward lukewarmness — toward being "neither cold nor hot."

The word’s fair use is against the child who turns every game into a war. Scripture opposes that too (Php 2:3). Teach both: try hard, gladly and without shame; and never let trying hard become an excuse to crush the joy of others. The zealous servant is not a sore winner.
roots_lines: Old French trier — to sift, pick out → English try, to attempt
usage: "Okay, tryhard, it’s just Uno."
Fervent in spirit, serving the Lord — be a tryhard at the right things (Rom 12:11).
Neither cold nor hot is the real insult (Rev 3:16).

etymology: Clipped from robot (from Czech robota, forced labor; Karel Capek’s play R.U.R., 1920). In games a bot is a computer-controlled player; when Fortnite added bots to new players’ lobbies in late 2019, Gen Alpha turned the word into an insult for a person who plays badly, predictably, or mindlessly — "you’re such a bot." It now means anyone judged clueless, and sits beside the related insult NPC.
biblical_def: Calling someone a bot means he plays like a computer — clumsy, predictable, easy to beat — or, more broadly, that he is clueless. "Bro is a bot" is a common Gen Alpha insult. The Christian observation: the insult works by turning a person into a machine, and Scripture forbids that move. Every person is made in God’s image: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him" (Gen 1:27). The same tongue that blesses God must not curse "men, which are made after the similitude of God" (Jas 3:9). To mock the weak player is to mock his Maker: "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker" (Pro 17:5). A bot has no soul; the boy you call a bot does, and Christ died for him. Jesus warned that contempt is a matter of the heart: "whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire" (Mat 5:22). A father can tell a five-year-old: "A bot is a computer, not a person. People are made by God, so we never call them names like that — even if they’re not good at the game yet." And he can teach the older child to see the "bot" in the lobby as a beginner to help.
webster_summary: Clip of robot; game AI player turned Gen Alpha insult (Fortnite, 2019) for a weak or clueless person — contempt that reduces an image-bearer to a machine.
webster_full: BOT, n. (clip of robot; gaming usage; Gen Alpha insult, 2019–present) A computer-controlled player; hence, a person who plays badly or acts mindlessly. "Stop being a bot."
Related insults: NPC, noob, default.
Other senses: social-media bots (automated accounts); chatbots.
Decode for parents: a mild-sounding word that carries real contempt.
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Jas 3:9
Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God.
Pro 17:5
Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished.
Mat 5:22

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
corruption_summary: Bot turns a weaker player into a machine; Scripture says every person bears God’s image, and contempt for him reproaches his Maker.
corruption_paragraphs: Dehumanizing language is easy when the other person is an avatar. The insult "bot" is meant as light trash talk, but its logic is that the other player is not really a person — just code to be farmed. Children practice that logic in game lobbies and carry it to the lunch table, where the "bot" is the kid who is slow, awkward, or new.

Answer with the image of God. Teach that every player behind every screen is a person, and that our words toward the weak reveal our hearts. Replace the insult with a habit: help the beginner, say "good game," and remember that God is mindful of the clumsy too.
roots_summary: Czech robota (forced labor) → robot (Capek, 1920) → bot (computing; game AI) → Gen Alpha insult (2019).
roots_lines: Late 2019: Fortnite adds AI bots to lobbies
usage: "Don’t call him a bot — he just started playing yesterday."
God created man in his own image — no bots in that lobby (Gen 1:27).
Whoso mocketh the poor player reproacheth his Maker (Pro 17:5).

etymology: From grief (sorrow, distress) through the older verb to grieve, to cause sorrow. In online games from the late 1990s (Ultima Online, then Second Life and others) a griefer was a player whose fun was ruining other people’s fun — killing new players, trapping them, destroying their work. Minecraft made griefing a household word for Gen Alpha: blowing up someone’s house with TNT, flooding it with lava, stealing from chests, or wrecking a server build. Many servers ban it outright.
biblical_def: To grief someone in a game is to ruin their stuff or their fun on purpose — blow up their Minecraft house, trap them, steal their things, just to watch them get upset. Gen Alpha children know the word because many of them have been griefed, and some have done it. The Christian observation: griefing is one of the clearest pictures of a sin Proverbs describes exactly: "It is as sport to a fool to do mischief" (Pro 10:23). And Proverbs has a sharper portrait still: "As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, so is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?" (Pro 26:18-19). "It’s just a game" is the griefer’s defense, and Scripture calls it the madman’s. The law of love runs the opposite way: "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour" (Rom 13:10). And the word’s own root warns us: the Holy Spirit can be grieved by the way we treat others — "grieve not the holy Spirit of God" (Eph 4:30), Paul says, in the middle of a passage about bitterness and evil speaking. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Breaking someone’s building on purpose makes them sad — and it makes God sad too. In our family we build each other up, not knock each other down."
webster_summary: Ruining others’ play on purpose (MMO slang, late 1990s; Minecraft household word) — mischief done as sport, the firebrand-throwing "am not I in sport?" of Proverbs.
webster_full: GRIEFING, n. / v. (online-game slang, late 1990s–present; Gen Alpha via Minecraft) Deliberately ruining other players’ work or enjoyment. "Someone griefed our base."
Griefer — one who griefs. To grief — to do it.
Common forms: TNT, lava, theft from chests, trapping, spawn-killing.
Decode for parents: there is no innocent version; the pleasure is in another’s distress.
Webster 1828, the root — GRIEF, n. The pain of mind produced by loss, misfortune, injury or evils of any kind; sorrow; regret.
scriptures: It is as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom.
As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death,
So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?
Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
Eph 4:30
And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.
corruption_summary: Griefing takes pleasure in another’s loss and calls it a game; Scripture calls it the fool’s sport and the madman’s "am not I in sport?"
corruption_paragraphs: Of all game behaviors, griefing is the one whose whole point is another’s sorrow. It is not competition (which has rules and a winner) but malice dressed as play. Children who learn to enjoy it are learning cruelty at low stakes, and the anonymity of a server removes the face that would ordinarily stop them.

Reject it plainly. Make it a household law: we never wreck what others build. If your child has been griefed, sit with the grief — it is real — and teach forgiveness. If he has griefed someone, teach restitution: go back, rebuild, apologize. Love worketh no ill, even on a server.
roots_summary: Latin gravis (heavy) → Old French grief → English grief, grieve → online-game griefer (late 1990s) → Minecraft griefing.
roots_lines: Latin gravis — heavy; gravare, to burden → Old French grever, grief
2010s Minecraft: griefing as a household word; anti-grief server rules
usage: "Somebody griefed my village with lava and I worked on it for a week."
It is as sport to a fool to do mischief (Pro 10:23).
Am not I in sport? — the griefer’s excuse, and the madman’s (Pro 26:19).

etymology: Gamer slang of the 2000s: to quit a game abruptly in anger — slamming the controller, closing the app, storming off. Viral videos of the period, most famously the "Angry German Kid" clip (2006), made rage-quitting a meme, and streamers’ on-camera meltdowns kept it alive. Gen Alpha uses "rage quit" for leaving any game, argument, or activity in a temper — and "he rage-quit" is a common report from the next room.
biblical_def: To rage quit is to stop playing because you are mad — throw the controller, slam the laptop, stomp away. Every Gen Alpha household has heard it, and many have seen it. The Christian observation: the rage quit is a small, honest picture of an angry heart. Scripture does not say that anger is never right, but it says it must be ruled. "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 4:26). James gives the order: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:19-20). And Proverbs notes what rage reveals: "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Pro 29:11). The rage quit is not a crime; it is a chance. It shows a child, and his father, where self-control is still missing. A father can tell a five-year-old: "It’s okay to feel mad when you lose. But we don’t throw things. We take a deep breath, ask God for help, and try again — or take a break and come back." And he can model it the next time he loses at something himself.
webster_summary: Gamer slang (2000s; "Angry German Kid," 2006) for quitting in a fury — a small honest picture of the unruled spirit, and a chance to teach the slow anger Proverbs praises.
webster_full: RAGE QUIT, v. / n. (gaming slang, 2000s–present; Gen Alpha) To quit a game abruptly in anger; such a quitting. "He rage-quit after the third loss."
Often accompanied by controller-throwing, yelling, or slammed devices.
Extended use: leaving any argument or activity in a temper.
Decode for parents: a window into your child’s self-control; treat it as training, not just discipline.
Webster 1828, the root — RAGE, n. Violent anger accompanied with furious words, gestures or agitation; anger excited to fury.
Webster 1828, the root — QUIT, v.t. To leave; to depart from, either temporarily or forever.
scriptures: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
Eph 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Jas 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
corruption_summary: The rage quit is the unruled spirit in miniature; Scripture does not forbid all anger, but it commands the anger that is slow, ruled, and settled before sundown.
corruption_paragraphs: Games are designed to produce frustration and reward — that is part of their pull — and children whose self-control is still forming meet that frustration many times an hour. The rage quit is the moment the spirit’s walls break. Left untrained, the habit carries into sports, school, and marriage: when it gets hard, explode and leave.

Use the moment. Do not only confiscate the controller; teach the child to name the anger, to breathe, to pray, and to come back. Praise the time he stays calm after a loss more than the time he wins. He that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city — or a Victory Royale.
roots_summary: Latin rabies (madness) → English rage + quit → 2000s gamer rage quit → Gen Alpha household report.
roots_lines: Latin quietus — at rest, free → English quit, to leave off
Streamer meltdowns keep the meme alive
usage: "Did you rage quit again?" "...Maybe."
He that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city (Pro 16:32).
Be angry, and sin not — and don’t throw the controller (Eph 4:26).

etymology: From the old English verb and noun lag, to fall behind, be slow (sixteenth century). In networked games, lag is the delay between a player’s action and the game’s response, caused by a slow connection; "laggy" means stuttering. Gen Alpha blames lag for every loss — "I lagged!" — and uses "lag" for any slowness, including a sibling who is slow to get the joke ("you’re lagging").
biblical_def: Lag is when a game freezes or delays because of a slow connection, and "I lagged!" is the most common excuse in Gen Alpha life: it explains every loss. The Christian observation: the word holds a small lesson about blaming. Sometimes the lag is real; often it is the oldest excuse in the world — it wasn’t me. Adam said, "The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree" (Gen 3:12); Eve said, "The serpent beguiled me" (Gen 3:13). Scripture’s way is honest confession: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Pro 28:13). And there is a sweeter lesson in the word. Everything in our world lags — connections, people, even our own hearts — but God never does. "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness" (2Pe 3:9); He is "a very present help in trouble" (Psa 46:1). He hears the instant we pray. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Sometimes games lag and get slow. But God never lags! When you talk to Him, He hears you right away." And to the older child after a loss: "Was it the lag, or was it me?" is a good question for a whole life.
webster_summary: Old word for falling behind (16th c.), now network delay in games and Gen Alpha’s universal excuse — a lesson in Adam’s blame-shifting and in the God who is never slack.
webster_full: LAG, n. / v. (English, 16th c.; networked-game usage, 1990s–present; Gen Alpha) Delay between action and response in an online game; to experience it. "The server is lagging so bad."
Laggy — stuttering, delayed. Lag spike — a sudden bad delay.
Extended use: slowness of any kind ("you’re lagging" = you’re slow to understand).
Decode for parents: sometimes real, often an excuse.
Webster 1828, the root — LAG, a. Coming after or behind; slow; sluggish; tardy.
scriptures: Gen 3:12
And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.
Gen 3:13
And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
Psa 46:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
corruption_summary: Lag is a real technical problem and a ready-made excuse; Scripture answers the excuse with confession and the delay with the God who is not slack.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no sin in a slow connection. The habit to watch is the reflex of blame: every loss is the lag’s fault, every mistake someone else’s. That reflex is as old as the garden, and games give children a hundred chances a day to rehearse it.

Teach the honest sentence: "I made a mistake." Praise it when you hear it. Then give the child the comfort the word points to: in a world that lags, God’s attention never buffers. He is a very present help.
roots_summary: Possibly Scandinavian or Celtic lag (last, slow; 16th c.) → to fall behind → networked-game lag (1990s) → Gen Alpha’s universal excuse.
roots_lines: 16th-c. English lag — the last; to fall behind (origin uncertain)
Gen Alpha: "I lagged!" as excuse; "you’re lagging" as tease
usage: "I didn’t lose — I lagged!"
The woman gave me, the serpent beguiled me, the lag got me — the oldest excuses (Gen 3:12-13).
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise — God never lags (2Pe 3:9).

etymology: From streaming culture: Twitch introduced "Clips" in 2016, letting viewers save a short segment of a live stream, and streamers began shouting "Clip it!" or "Clip that!" when something funny, impressive, or embarrassing happened so their fans would save and share it. Gen Alpha uses the phrase in real life — "clip that!" when a friend trips, says something dumb, or makes an amazing shot — with the implication that the moment should be recorded and posted.
biblical_def: "Clip it!" means "Somebody record that!" — shouted when a friend does something amazing or, more often, something embarrassing. In Gen Alpha life the phone is always nearby, and the phrase is half joke and half real. The Christian observation: the word asks what we save and share about each other. Scripture has a whole wisdom about this. "He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends" (Pro 17:9). "Above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1Pe 4:8). A friend’s embarrassing moment, clipped and posted, is the opposite of covering: it repeats the matter to the whole world, forever. And the Bible’s way with a brother’s fault is private first: "go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone" (Mat 18:15). But there is a beautiful kind of clipping too. God keeps a record of the good His people do: "a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name" (Mal 3:16). A father can tell a five-year-old: "We don’t record people when they’re embarrassed — that’s not kind. But when someone does something good, we can tell everybody! God remembers all the good things His children do."
webster_summary: Streamer shout from Twitch Clips (2016-) carried into real life — "record that!" — and a question of what we save about one another: Scripture covers the transgression and remembers the good.
webster_full: CLIP IT, interj. (streaming slang, 2016–present; Gen Alpha) Save or record that moment. Also clip that. "He fell off the swing — clip it!"
From Twitch Clips (2016), the feature for saving segments of live streams.
Decode for parents: often harmless, but it can be the first step of posting a classmate’s humiliation.

Webster 1828, the root — CLIP, v.t. To cut off with shears or scissors; to separate by a sudden stroke; especially to cut off the ends or sides of a thing, to make it shorter or narrower, in distinction from shaving and paring, which are performed by rubbing the instrument close to the thing shaved; as, to clip the hair; to clip wings.
scriptures: Pro 17:9
He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.
Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
corruption_summary: "Clip it" treats a neighbor’s worst moment as content to save and share; Scripture covers the transgression in love and keeps its book of remembrance for the good.
corruption_paragraphs: Children now grow up in a world where any moment can become permanent and public. "Clip it" is the reflex of that world: the instinct to capture another’s stumble for an audience. Most of the time it is a joke; some of the time it is the start of a humiliation that follows a child for years.

Teach the covering instinct. In our house we do not record people at their worst; we protect each other’s dignity. Then teach the remembering instinct: notice and tell the good — the kind act, the brave word. The family that clips each other’s virtues is imitating Malachi 3:16.
roots_summary: Old Norse klippa (to cut) → English clip → video clip → Twitch Clips (2016) → "clip it!" in streaming and real life.
roots_lines: Old Norse klippa — to cut → English clip, to cut short
20th c.: a film or video clip
usage: "Clip that! He made it from half court!"
He that covereth a transgression seeketh love — don’t clip the fall (Pro 17:9).
God keeps a book of remembrance — clip the good (Mal 3:16).

etymology: From English edit, to revise or prepare for publication (back-formed from editor, eighteenth century). As a Gen Alpha noun, an edit is a short fan-made video montage — clips of an athlete, anime character, movie hero, or "sigma" figure cut to music (often phonk), with slow motion, flashes, and transitions — made in apps like CapCut (2020) and posted to TikTok and YouTube Shorts. "That’s so edit" or "edit-worthy" praises a dramatic moment; "velocity edit" names the speed-ramp style. In Fortnite, "edit" also means reshaping a built wall.
biblical_def: An edit is a fast, dramatic fan video — a hero’s best moments cut to pounding music, slow-mo, and flashes. Gen Alpha children watch hundreds of them, and many make their own. The Christian observation: an edit is the art of showing only the glory. It cuts away the boring parts, the failures, the ordinary days, and leaves a person looking like a god. That is an old human habit with an old name in Scripture: idolatry — giving a creature the glory that belongs to the Creator. "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1Jn 5:21). The edit also trains a child to see her own life as a highlight reel and to be disappointed with the uncut version. But God sees the whole film, and He loves it: "we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal" (2Co 4:18). And the best "edit" in the world is not ours but God’s — "whatsoever things are true... honest... just... pure... lovely... think on these things" (Php 4:8). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Videos only show the cool parts. But God sees all of you — even the boring and the hard parts — and He loves the whole you."
webster_summary: Fan-made music montage of a hero’s highlights (CapCut era, 2020-) — the art of showing only the glory, which tilts toward idolizing people and editing one’s own life into a highlight reel.
webster_full: EDIT, n. (Gen Alpha / Gen-Z usage, c. 2020–present) A short fan-made video montage of clips set to music, often phonk, with dramatic effects. "Did you see the Messi edit?"
Styles: velocity edit, sigma edit, anime edit, phonk edit.
Fortnite sense: to reshape a built wall, floor, or ramp ("fast edits").
Decode for parents: notice who the edits glorify; children imitate the figures they watch edited.
Webster 1828, the root — EDIT, v.t. Properly, to publish; more usually, to superintend a publication; to prepare a book or paper for the public eye, by writing, correcting or selecting the matter.
scriptures: Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.
While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.
corruption_summary: The edit cuts a life down to its glory shots and sets it to a beat; it trains children to idolize the edited and to despise their own uncut lives.
corruption_paragraphs: Edits are a powerful form of persuasion. The figures they glorify — often brooding, violent, or vain characters — are given the soundtrack of triumph, and children absorb the message that this is what greatness looks like. "They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them" (Psa 115:8): what we watch exalted, we become.

Teach your child to ask of every edit: who is being glorified, and for what? Then let him make edits of better things — a family trip, a brother’s goal, a grandfather’s stories. The craft is not evil; the worship is. And remind him that God loves his uncut life.
roots_summary: Latin edere (to put forth, publish) → editor → back-formed edit (18th c.) → Gen Alpha edit, a fan montage (c. 2020).
roots_lines: 2020: CapCut and short-video apps make montage-editing easy
Gen Alpha noun: an edit; styles velocity, sigma, phonk
usage: "I made an edit of our dog with phonk music. He looks so sigma."
Little children, keep yourselves from idols — even edited ones (1Jn 5:21).
The things which are seen are temporal — God loves the uncut version (2Co 4:18).

etymology: A respelling of funk. The style descends from 1990s Memphis underground rap — lo-fi cassette tapes, eerie samples, chanted hooks, and often horror-themed or occult lyrics — revived on SoundCloud in the 2010s under the name phonk. Around 2020–22 a faster, cowbell-heavy, bass-distorted offshoot called "drift phonk," much of it produced by Russian and Brazilian artists, became the soundtrack of car videos, gym clips, and above all edits; for Gen Alpha, phonk is "the edit music."
biblical_def: Phonk is the pounding, cowbell-and-bass music Gen Alpha hears behind sports edits, anime edits, and "sigma" videos. It is built to make anything look intense. The Christian observation: music is never neutral; it is one of God’s most powerful gifts for shaping the heart. When an evil spirit troubled Saul, David "took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well" (1Sa 16:23). God’s people are told to fill their mouths and minds with music that builds up: "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" (Eph 5:19); "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (Col 3:16). Phonk’s roots are in a Memphis underground that often dwelt on horror, violence, and the occult, and much drift phonk loops dark samples behind its beat. Most of it has few words; the question is what mood it trains and what images it is married to. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Music can make us feel all kinds of ways. God gave us songs to make our hearts happy and brave in Him. Let’s play some of those." Then he plays something better loud.
webster_summary: Respelled funk: Memphis underground rap (1990s) revived on SoundCloud (2010s) and reborn as cowbell "drift phonk" (2020–22), the soundtrack of Gen Alpha edits — music that forms moods, from roots that often dwelt in darkness.
webster_full: PHONK, n. (music genre; Memphis roots 1990s; SoundCloud 2010s; drift phonk 2020–present) Lo-fi or distorted rap-derived music with cowbells, heavy bass, and eerie samples; the standard soundtrack of edits. "Put phonk on the edit."
Subgenres: Memphis phonk, drift phonk, Brazilian phonk.
Decode for parents: mostly instrumental; check the samples and the images it is paired with.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: Phonk is mood-music for the edit, descended from an underground that dwelt on horror and the occult; Scripture treats music as heart-shaping and fills the house with psalms and hymns.
corruption_paragraphs: The genre’s effect is its point: menace, swagger, intensity. Married to edits of violent characters or "sigma" posturing, it teaches children to feel that coldness and aggression are thrilling. Its Memphis ancestors traded openly in dark and occult imagery, and some of that DNA survives in the samples. A child does not need lyrics to be shaped by a sound.

Do not merely ban; replace. Fill the car and the kitchen with music that is strong and good — the psalms sung, hymns with drums, songs that make a child feel brave in God. David’s harp drove the darkness from Saul’s tent. Music is a weapon; hand your child the right one.
roots_summary: Funk → 1990s Memphis underground rap → SoundCloud phonk (2010s) → drift phonk (2020–22) → the edit soundtrack.
roots_lines: American English funk — a musical style (and older: a strong smell)
1990s: Memphis underground cassette rap, often horror-themed
2020–22: drift phonk — cowbells, distorted 808s; Russian and Brazilian producers
usage: "This edit needs more phonk."
David took an harp and played, and Saul was refreshed — music shapes the soul (1Sa 16:23).
Psalms and hymns and spiritual songs — that’s the playlist (Eph 5:19).

etymology: From live-stream chat culture of the late 2010s and 2020s, where viewers spam the letter W (for "win") to celebrate a streamer’s success and L (for "loss") to mock a failure. "Drop a W in the chat" or "Ws in the chat" became a streamer’s call for applause, and Gen Alpha uses it out loud at school and home to cheer for someone: a friend’s good grade, a sister’s goal, a dad’s pancake flip.
biblical_def: "Ws in the chat!" means "Everybody cheer!" — it is the Gen Alpha way of saying "Give it up for him!" It comes from live-stream chats where people type W for "win." The Christian observation: this is one of the redeemable words, because it is a call to celebrate someone else. Scripture commands exactly that: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice" (Rom 12:15). The church is meant to be a room full of Ws for one another: "Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another" (1Th 5:11); "exhort one another daily, while it is called To day" (Heb 3:13). Good words are a gift: "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" (Pro 16:24). The phrase’s twin, "Ls in the chat," is the opposite — a pile-on of mockery — and that is the one to leave behind. A father can tell a five-year-old: "When your brother does something good, we put Ws in the chat — we cheer for him! God loves it when we’re happy for each other." A family that hands out Ws at dinner is practicing 1 Thessalonians 5:11 without knowing it.
webster_summary: Live-stream chat call to cheer ("drop a W") carried into Gen Alpha speech — a redeemable habit of rejoicing with them that rejoice, opposite its twin "Ls in the chat."
webster_full: Ws IN THE CHAT, interj. / phr. (streaming slang, late 2010s–present; Gen Alpha) A call to celebrate someone’s success. "She got first place — Ws in the chat!"
Variants: drop a W, big W, W rizz. Opposite: Ls in the chat (mockery).
From viewers spamming W (win) and L (loss) in live-stream chats.
Decode for parents: one of the kind ones — encourage it, and watch for its L twin.
Webster 1828, the root — CHAT, v.i. To talk in a familiar manner; to talk without form or ceremony.
scriptures: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do.
Heb 3:13
But exhort one another daily , while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.
corruption_summary: "Ws in the chat" is a call to celebrate another, which Scripture commands; its only corruption is its twin, the pile-on of Ls.
corruption_paragraphs: Little to correct here. The habit of public cheering is good, and the phrase invites children to notice and praise one another. The caution is the mirror phrase — "Ls in the chat" — in which a crowd piles mockery on someone who failed. Both come from the same chat culture, and children use both.

Keep the W, drop the L. Make cheering for siblings a household custom. Rejoice with them that rejoice; edify one another; let pleasant words be honeycomb. A boy who learns to type W for his brother is learning to love his brother’s good.
roots_summary: Live-stream chat: W (win) / L (loss) spam (late 2010s) → "drop a W," "Ws in the chat" → Gen Alpha spoken cheer.
roots_lines: Late 2010s: Twitch and YouTube chat spam of Ws and Ls
Streamer calls: "drop a W in the chat"
2020s: spoken aloud by Gen Alpha as a cheer
usage: "Mom made the best tacos ever — Ws in the chat!"
Rejoice with them that do rejoice — Ws in the chat (Rom 12:15).
Edify one another: hand out Ws at the dinner table (1Th 5:11).

etymology: L ("loss," from sports standings and stream-chat spam) + bozo (a fool, American slang from the 1920s, reinforced by Bozo the Clown, created in 1946). The taunt "L + ratio + bozo" spread on Twitter around 2021 as a dismissive reply, and Gen Alpha shortened it to "L bozo": "you lost, clown." It is said to anyone who fails, gets something wrong, or simply disagrees.
biblical_def: "L bozo" means "You lost, clown." Gen Alpha children say it to a friend who misses a shot, gets a wrong answer, or loses a game — sometimes as a joke, often to sting. The Christian observation: the phrase is a pocket-sized insult, and Scripture takes insults far more seriously than children do. Jesus said, "whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire" (Mat 5:22). "Bozo" is simply "thou fool" with a clown nose on. The rule for a Christian mouth is plain: "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29). "He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth" (Pro 14:21), and the man who mocks the one who stumbles is the man Proverbs warns (Pro 17:5). A father can tell a five-year-old: "When someone loses, we don’t call them names. We say ‘good try’ or ‘you’ll get it next time.’ Jesus says our words should help people, not hurt them." Then he can give the better phrase from the same language: put Ws in the chat instead.
webster_summary: "Loss" + "bozo" (fool, clown) — Twitter’s "L + ratio + bozo" (c. 2021) shortened to a Gen Alpha taunt; "thou fool" with a clown nose, which Jesus does not find funny.
webster_full: L BOZO, interj. (internet slang, c. 2021–present; Gen Alpha) A taunt: you lost, you fool. "You missed? L bozo."
Fuller form: L + ratio + bozo.
Bozo — American slang for a fool (1920s); Bozo the Clown (1946).
Decode for parents: a mockery word; replace rather than tolerate.
Webster 1828, the root — CLOWN, n. A countryman; a rustic; hence, one who has the manners of a rustic; a churl; a man of coarse manners; an ill-bred man.
scriptures: Mat 5:22

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he.
Pro 17:5
Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished.
corruption_summary: "L bozo" kicks the fallen and calls him a fool; Scripture counts "thou fool" a grave sin of the tongue and commands words that minister grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Trash talk is old, but internet culture has made the casual insult constant and reflexive. "L bozo" is said a dozen times a day in some classrooms, and its target is always the one who just failed — the moment a child most needs grace. The habit forms a heart that meets weakness with contempt.

Reject the phrase and give a replacement. Teach Eph 4:29 as a family motto. When your child is the one called bozo, comfort him; when he is the one saying it, correct him and have him say something kind to the same friend. A tongue trained to bless the loser is a Christian tongue.
roots_summary: L (loss) + bozo (fool, 1920s; Bozo the Clown, 1946) → "L + ratio + bozo" (Twitter, c. 2021) → Gen Alpha "L bozo."
roots_lines: Bozo — American slang for a fool (1920s; origin uncertain)
usage: "L bozo!" "Hey — we don’t say that. Say good try."
Whosoever shall say, Thou fool — or bozo — shall be in danger (Mat 5:22).
Let your words minister grace unto the hearers (Eph 4:29).
